newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Budapest bourse edges lower despite Wall St rally.
newsitem.headline: Budapest bourse edges lower despite Wall St rally.

text.p: The Budapest Stock Exchange lost ground on a mixed market on Tuesday, failing to hammer advantage from Wall Street's two percent gain, traders said.
"It was somewhat strange that the market fell despite the fact that foreign markets rose and that there was no bad news about the Hungarian market," said Andrea Keresztesi of ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett.
The BUX index finished at a preliminary 5,864.43 points, down 38.06.
Activity also may have been somewhat muted by funds tied up in subscription for the IPO for oil company MOL, whose pricing is due to be announced any day, traders said.
Analysts said the market was fairly priced and the remaining batch of first quarter figures will give mixed signals.

"It's moving basically sideways because there's not much to go forward in terms of the value of the companies and I suspect that the rest of the Q1 figures will be mixed," said Frances Cloud of Nomura Equity Research in London.
But the market's longer-term outlook was positive, other analysts said.

"The BUX index is in the second stage of a three stage cycle that will lead the index higher over the next 18 months," Mark Kane, analyst at MC-BBL securities house, said in a technical analysis, dated April 30th and received on Tuesday.
"Providing the index can hold above 5,750 points an advance of up to 15 percent could follow," he said.
On Tuesday once again MOL was the most actively traded paper with nearly 600,000 shares traded. MOL closed at 3,220 forints, up 20, rebounding from Monday's roughly five percent fall.
"Mostly domestic investors were buying the papers, they were apparently not influenced by the news of the doubled amount of shares on offer," ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett's Keresztesi said.
The domestic offer of MOL shares, originally set at one plus one percent, has been increased to one plus three percent.
The Hungarian bourse has traditionally been driven by foreign investors but analysts said an increasing number of domestic investors are trying to be part of the market.
Cloud said that most foreign investors have stopped putting money into central Europe.

"They're not taking money out but nor are they significantly adding to their holdings," she said. "The main influence...to the Budapest market now appears to be domestic investors which is quite a new phenomenon."
Elsewhere on the market, pharmaceuticals Egis gave up 150 forints to end at 11,000, while chemicals Borsodchem edged up five forints to 6,600.
The market's other chemicals TVK fell 60 forints to 2,850 forints in what Keresztesi attributed to profit-taking by domestic investors.
Some illiquid stocks, including mineral water bottler Kekkuti and retailer Aranypok, rose more than four percent to 1,100 forints and 8,300 forints, respectively.

In one single deal 50,000 shares in retailer Csopak changed hands, representing almost two percent in the company's 2.45 billion forint share capital. In that one deal it traded at 2,800 forints, up 50.
